items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water in a plant.

rubric.why: Shows why transpiration is harmful to the plant.
rubric.description: Transpiration causes loss of water, which can lead to wilting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water loss and its harmful effect, such as wilting or dehydration.

rubric.why: Shows why transpiration is also useful or necessary.
rubric.description: Transpiration helps in the ascent of sap and/or cools the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating a useful function of transpiration.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant; excessive water loss may cause wilting or dehydration.
It is necessary because it helps in the ascent of sap and cools the plant.

items.followUp: Compare diffusion and osmosis with respect to energy use and direction of movement.

rubric.why: Identifies that active transport requires energy and can move substances against a concentration gradient.
rubric.description: Active transport requires energy and may move substances from lower to higher concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both energy requirement and movement against the concentration gradient.

rubric.why: Distinguishes passive transport from active transport.
rubric.description: Passive transport does not require energy and moves substances down the concentration gradient.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both no energy requirement and movement down the concentration gradient.

modelAnswer: Active transport requires energy, usually from ATP, and can move substances from a lower to a higher concentration.
Passive transport does not require energy and moves substances from a higher to a lower concentration.

items.followUp: State the rules for writing a scientific name using binomial nomenclature and give an example.

rubric.why: Defines the two-part form of a scientific name.
rubric.description: A scientific name consists of two words: the genus name followed by the species name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the two names and their order.

rubric.why: Includes the language convention for scientific names.
rubric.description: The names are Latin or Latinised.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the names are Latin or Latinised.

rubric.why: Includes the writing or printing convention.
rubric.description: The two words are italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct convention.

rubric.why: Includes the capitalisation convention for the two names.
rubric.description: The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both capitalisation rules.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming each organism with a two-word scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
The names are Latin or Latinised.
In print, both words are italicised; when handwritten, they are underlined separately.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a lowercase letter; for example, *Homo sapiens*.

items.followUp: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion and explain how its structure relates to its function.

rubric.why: Identifies the chloroplast's enclosing membranes.
rubric.description: A chloroplast is surrounded by a double membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it has an outer and an inner membrane.

rubric.why: Names the main internal regions and membrane structures.
rubric.description: The fluid stroma contains stacks of thylakoids called grana.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stroma and grana or thylakoids.

rubric.why: Links chlorophyll to the light-absorbing membranes.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll is present in the thylakoid membranes, which are arranged in grana.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for locating chlorophyll in thylakoids or grana.

rubric.why: States the role of the thylakoids in photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the light reaction and its location.

rubric.why: States a further role of the chloroplast, including the reactions in the stroma or food production.
rubric.description: The stroma is the site of carbon dioxide fixation in the light-independent reactions; photosynthesis produces carbohydrates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stroma's role in carbon dioxide fixation or for stating that photosynthesis produces food.

modelAnswer: A chloroplast is surrounded by an outer and an inner membrane.
Its interior contains a fluid matrix called the stroma and flattened membrane sacs called thylakoids, arranged in stacks called grana.
Chlorophyll is present in the thylakoid membranes and absorbs light energy.
The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis occur on the thylakoid membranes.
The light-independent reactions use carbon dioxide in the stroma to form carbohydrates.

items.followUp: Give two dietary sources of proteins and describe two functions of proteins in the body.

rubric.why: Identifies dietary sources of proteins.
rubric.description: Protein sources include meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses, beans and nuts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least two valid sources.

rubric.why: States the role of proteins in body growth and tissue maintenance.
rubric.description: Proteins are needed for growth and repair of body tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for growth and/or tissue repair.

rubric.why: Identifies another important role of proteins.
rubric.description: Proteins form enzymes, antibodies and some hormones.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least one valid protein role or product.

rubric.why: Recognises an additional function or protein-based body component.
rubric.description: Proteins can be used as an energy source and form structures or substances such as muscles and haemoglobin.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid additional function or protein-based component.

modelAnswer: Sources of proteins include meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses, beans and nuts.
Proteins are needed for the growth and repair of body tissues.
They form enzymes, antibodies and some hormones.
They also form body structures such as muscles; proteins can be used as an energy source when needed.

items.followUp: Explain the lock-and-key model of enzyme action and compare it with the induced-fit model.

rubric.why: Describes the specific fit proposed by the lock-and-key model.
rubric.description: In the lock-and-key model, the substrate fits the enzyme's active site because their shapes are complementary.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the complementary fit of substrate and active site.

rubric.why: Identifies formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the complex forms.

rubric.why: Explains the defining feature of the induced-fit model.
rubric.description: In the induced-fit model, binding of the substrate causes the active site to change shape slightly to fit it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that substrate binding changes the active site's shape.

rubric.why: Describes conversion of substrate into product.
rubric.description: The enzyme catalyses the reaction and the products are released.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate is converted to products and released.

rubric.why: Shows that the enzyme is not used up by the reaction.
rubric.description: The enzyme remains unchanged and can be reused.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the enzyme remains unchanged or can be reused.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, the substrate has a shape complementary to the enzyme's active site and fits into it.
An enzyme-substrate complex forms; the enzyme catalyses the reaction and the products are released.
In the induced-fit model, the active site is flexible: the substrate binding causes it to change shape slightly to fit the substrate.
The enzyme converts the substrate into products, which are released from the active site.
The enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.

items.followUp: Explain how the movement of ions and water into and out of guard cells controls stomatal opening and closing.

rubric.why: Identifies a key event that initiates stomatal opening.
rubric.description: In light, potassium ions enter the guard cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the light-associated uptake of potassium ions by guard cells.

rubric.why: Connects water uptake and increased guard-cell turgidity to opening.
rubric.description: Water enters the guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid and the stomatal pore opens.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for water uptake by osmosis and the resulting opening.

rubric.why: Identifies a key event that initiates stomatal closing.
rubric.description: In darkness, potassium ions leave the guard cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the loss of potassium ions from guard cells.

rubric.why: Connects water loss and reduced guard-cell turgidity to closing.
rubric.description: Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis; they become flaccid and the pore closes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for water loss by osmosis and the resulting closing.

modelAnswer: In light, potassium ions enter the guard cells, lowering their water potential.
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis, making them turgid; the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, potassium ions leave the guard cells, raising their water potential.
Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, making them flaccid; the stomatal pore closes.

items.followUp: Describe how a microspore develops into a pollen grain and how a megaspore develops into an embryo sac.

rubric.why: Describes meiosis and formation of the functional megaspore.
rubric.description: The megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores; usually three degenerate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for meiosis producing four megaspores and identifying the functional survivor or degeneration of the other three.

rubric.why: Describes nuclear division during embryo-sac development.
rubric.description: The functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions to produce eight nuclei.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for three mitotic divisions producing eight nuclei.

rubric.why: Identifies the mature embryo-sac arrangement.
rubric.description: The mature embryo sac has an egg apparatus, three antipodal cells and a central cell with two polar nuclei.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the main cell types and polar nuclei.

rubric.why: Describes the origin of pollen grains from microspores.
rubric.description: A microspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of four microspores.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for meiosis forming a tetrad or four microspores.

rubric.why: Describes the cells formed as a microspore develops into a pollen grain.
rubric.description: A microspore divides by mitosis to form a tube (vegetative) cell and a generative cell; the generative cell later forms two male gametes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the two pollen-cell types or for stating that the generative cell forms two male gametes.

modelAnswer: In the ovule, a megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores; usually three degenerate and one remains functional.
The functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, producing eight nuclei.
These form a seven-celled embryo sac: an egg cell, two synergids, three antipodal cells and a central cell containing two polar nuclei.
In the anther, a microspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of four microspores.
Each microspore divides by mitosis to form a tube (vegetative) cell and a generative cell; the generative cell later divides to form two male gametes.
